sentences.text: Ctenoptychius is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish belonging to the order Petalodontiformes, named for its comb-folded appearance.
The type species C. apicalis is known mainly from flattened, serrated teeth, though some poorly preserved specimens show the head, pectoral fins, and body scales.
Its body was depressiform, meaning it was flattened, and featured large, broad pectoral fins.
The tooth crowns of C. apicalis featured between three and nine small cusp-like structures called cusplets, with the central one being the largest.
The holotype tooth of the type species C. apicalis is currently missing.
Based on available fossils, Ctenoptychius is believed to have had a flattened, ray-like body.
Articulated body fossils of Ctenoptychius apicalis were first described from the North Staffordshire Coalfield in 1890.
Fossils suggest Ctenoptychius lived in shallow marine environments and likely fed as an omnivorous bottom feeder on hard-shelled invertebrates.
Ctenoptychius belongs to the family Belantseidae.
The genus is classified within the class Chondrichthyes, which includes cartilaginous fish.
C. apicalis lived during the Late Carboniferous period, with fossils found in the United Kingdom and potentially the United States.
The genus Ctenoptychius existed from the Serpukhovian to the Kungurian stages, between 330.3 and 274.4 million years ago.
The status of C. korni is debated; it has been assigned to Ctenoptychius or Janassa, but some researchers suggest it belongs to neither genus due to lacking distinctive features of both.
